sets.bigIdea: A preposition plus its object makes a phrase, and the phrase does one of three jobs: tells you how or where about a verb, tells you which one about a noun, or stands as the noun itself. The preposition’s meaning shifts with the case of its object.
sets.masterMnemonic: How · Which · What — then one case, two cases, three.
sets.masterMnemonicWhy: First the phrase’s job: How (adverbial, it hangs on a verb), Which (adjectival, it hangs on a noun), What (substantival, it is the noun). Then the seventeen, sorted by how many cases they take: eight take one, six take two, and the three P’s — ἐπί, παρά, πρός — take all three.
sets.scene: A bridge 🌉 with everything happening around it: over it, under it, through it, from it, beside it.

groups.name: What the phrase does
groups.mnemonic: How · Which · What — hangs on a verb, hangs on a noun, or is the noun.
groups.expand: Adverbial (modifies a verb) · Adjectival (modifies a noun) · Substantival (acts as a noun)
groups.scene: Three signs on the bridge 🧩: an arrow ➡️ to the verb for how, a label 🏷️ on the noun for which, and a crate 📦 that simply is the thing.

groups.name: Takes one case
groups.key: ἀνά · ἀντί · ἀπό · εἰς · ἐκ · ἐν · πρό · σύν
groups.mnemonic: Eight take one case. Genitive ones go away, accusative ones go toward, dative ones stay put.
groups.expand: Genitive: ἀντί, ἀπό, ἐκ, πρό · Accusative: ἀνά, εἰς · Dative: ἐν, σύν
groups.scene: Eight on the bridge, each holding one case 1️⃣: four walking off it with the genitive (from, out of, instead of, before) 🚶, two walking onto it with the accusative (into, up) ➡️, two sitting still on it with the dative (in, with) 🪑.

groups.name: Takes two cases
groups.key: διά · κατά · μετά · περί · ὑπέρ · ὑπό
groups.mnemonic: Six take two, and always the same two: genitive and accusative.
groups.expand: διά through / because of · κατά against / according to · μετά with / after · περί concerning / around · ὑπέρ for, above · ὑπό by, under
groups.scene: Six with two faces each 2️⃣ — genitive on one side, accusative on the other. None of the six ever takes a dative.

groups.name: Takes three cases
groups.mnemonic: The three P’s take all three cases: ἐπί, παρά, πρός.
groups.expand: ἐπί on / upon / against · παρά from / with / beside · πρός for / at / to
groups.scene: Three at the end of the bridge 3️⃣, every one with a π in it, every one taking genitive, dative and accusative.

sets.name: Conjunction
sets.does: joins words, clauses and sentences
sets.subtitle: Joiners. Either two equals side by side, or one clause hung on another.
sets.eli5: Glue words. “And”, “but”, “so”, “because”, “if”. They stick two bits of a sentence together and say how the bits fit.
sets.bigIdea: Two kinds of joint. A coordinating conjunction joins equals — and, or, but, so, for. A subordinating one hangs a clause on another and says why: purpose, result, cause, comparison, condition, concession, content, time or place.
sets.masterMnemonic: And · Or · But · So · For — then the nine ways to hang one clause on another.
sets.masterMnemonicWhy: The five coordinating types are just the five English joiners: And (copulative), Or (disjunctive), But (adversative), So (inferential), For (explanatory). The nine subordinating ones are the English you would use: In order that, So that, Because, As, If, Even if, That, When, Where.
sets.scene: A railway junction 🚉, where lines join. Some run side by side as equals; some branch off the main line.

groups.name: Side by side — coordinating
groups.mnemonic: And · Or · But · So · For — five joiners, two equal clauses.
groups.expand: Copulative (and) · Disjunctive (or) · Adversative (but) · Inferential (so) · Explanatory (for)
groups.scene: Two tracks side by side 🛤️: a coupling ➕ and, points 🔀 or, a buffer 🛑 but, a signal ➡️ so, and a timetable 📋 for — here is why.

groups.name: Branch lines — subordinating
groups.key: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where
groups.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — nine branch lines off the main one.
groups.expand: Purpose · Result · Causal · Comparative · Conditional · Concessive · Declarative · Temporal · Local
groups.scene: Nine branch lines 🔀: a target 🎯 in order that, a crash 💥 so that, a root 🌱 because, twins 👯 as, a fork 🚦 if, a shrug 🤷 even if, a speech bubble 💬 that, a clock ⏰ when, a pin 📍 where.

sets.name: Adverb
sets.does: tells when, how much, how and where
sets.subtitle: Says more about a verb, an adjective, or another adverb.
sets.eli5: A word that tells you more about the doing. Did it SECRETLY. Came AFTERWARD. Sit HERE. Or it turns up the volume on a describing word: VERY early.
sets.bigIdea: An adverb answers one of four questions — when, how much, how, where — about a verb, an adjective or another adverb. And now and then, with an article, it borrows a noun’s or an adjective’s job.
sets.masterMnemonic: When · How much · How · Where.
sets.masterMnemonicWhy: Four questions, four uses, in the chart’s order: Time, Degree, Manner, Place. Before that, ask what it hangs on — a verb in any mood, an adjective, or another adverb. After it, one twist: put an article in front and an adverb can act as a noun or an adjective.
sets.scene: A toolbox 🧰 of adjusters: a clock, a volume knob, a spirit level and a map pin, for tuning whatever you fit them to.

groups.name: What it hangs on
groups.mnemonic: Verb · Adjective · Adverb — it tunes a doing-word, a describing word, or another tuner.
groups.expand: A verb in any mood · an adjective · another adverb
groups.scene: Three things on the workbench 🔧: a motor ⚙️ (a verb, in any mood), a paint tin 🎨 (an adjective), and a spare knob 🎛️ (another adverb).

groups.name: The question it answers
groups.mnemonic: When · How much · How · Where — four questions an adverb answers.
groups.expand: Time · Degree · Manner · Place
groups.scene: Four gauges on the lid ❔: a clock 🕰️ when, a volume knob 🔊 how much, a spirit level 🎚️ how, and a map pin 📌 where.

groups.name: Wearing another hat
groups.mnemonic: Noun · Adjective — with an article in front, an adverb can do either job.
groups.expand: Substantival (τὸ ἐκτός, “the outside”) · Adjectival (ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ, “at the present time”)
groups.scene: Two borrowed hats 🎩 on the peg: an article turns ἐκτός “outside” into a thing, the outside 📦, and tucks νῦν “now” between article and noun, where only an adjective ever sits 🏷️.

sets.name: Particle
sets.does: says yes, amen, look, woe
sets.subtitle: Little words that add force, or grab your attention.
sets.eli5: Tiny words you would shout. “Yes!” “Amen!” “Look!” “Oh!” They do not change what the sentence says; they change how loud it is.
sets.bigIdea: A particle adds force or grabs attention, and leaves the grammar of the sentence alone. Intensifying particles say “yes, truly”; attention particles say “look!” and are really interjections.
sets.masterMnemonic: Yes! · Look!
sets.masterMnemonicWhy: Two kinds, two shouts. Yes! — intensification: ναί, ἀμήν, γέ. Look! — attention: ἰδού, οὐαί, ὦ.
sets.scene: The town crier rings his bell 🔔 and shouts. He adds nothing to the news — he only makes you hear it.

groups.name: The two shouts
groups.mnemonic: Yes · Look — turn it up, or turn your head.
groups.expand: Intensification (ναί, ἀμήν, γέ) · Attention (ἰδού, οὐαί, ὦ)
groups.scene: The crier has two shouts 🔔: “Yes! Amen!” 🙌 to turn the volume up, and “Look! Woe! O!” 👀 to make the crowd turn round.

cards.name: Subject
cards.eli5: Who is doing it. “John talks.” Who talks? John.
cards.oneLine: The one doing the verb.
cards.mnemonic: The subject wears the crown.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The nominative names, and the crown sits on whoever the verb is about. One verb, one nominative — that one is wearing it.
cards.spotIt: Ask the verb: who or what? That is your subject.
cards.bookDef: The subject of a finite verb.

examples.english: *John* bears witness about him
examples.note: John is nominative and does the witnessing. As plain as it gets.

examples.english: *Ivan* came to class.
examples.note: One verb, one nominative. Nothing tricky.

cards.name: Predicate Nominative
cards.eli5: “X is Y” puts X inside Y, like a box. The Word goes in the God box. Not the other way round.
cards.oneLine: Two nominatives with “is” between them. The second says what the first is.
cards.mnemonic: The subject is the small circle; the predicate is the big one.
cards.mnemonicWhy: “Is” looks like an equals sign, but it only points one way. “The Word was God” puts the Word inside God, not God inside the Word. Small circle inside a big one.
cards.spotIt: Find a form of “to be” — εἰμί, γίνομαι, ὑπάρχω — with a nominative on each side of it.
cards.bookDef: Provides further information about the subject as a complement of a copulative verb (expressing a state of being).
cards.watchOut: Apposition looks the same but has no verb. A verb makes a claim. A comma only makes a label.

examples.english: and the Word was *God*
examples.note: ὁ λόγος has the article, so it is the subject. θεός is what is said about it.

examples.english: God is *love*
examples.note: ὁ θεός has the article, so it is the subject. Love is what is said about him.

examples.english: for he himself is *our peace*
examples.note: αὐτός is a pronoun, so it takes the subject slot. See the pecking order.

examples.english: the Word became *flesh*
examples.note: ἐγένετο is a “became” verb, which counts. σάρξ is what is said about the Word.

cards.name: The Pecking Order
cards.eli5: Two words both look like the doer. Pick like picking teams: “he” words first, then “the” words, then names.

formula.note: First yes wins. John 1:1c: no pronoun, ὁ λόγος has the article — so it is the subject.

cards.oneLine: Two nominatives, one “is”. This is how you tell which one is the subject.
cards.mnemonic: PAP — ask Papa who is in charge.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Pronoun, then Article, then Proper name. Papa answers in that order every time.
cards.spotIt: Go down the list and stop at the first yes.
cards.watchOut: No article does not mean “a”. A predicate noun sitting in front of the verb normally drops it.

examples.english: and the Word was God
examples.note: No pronoun, so the article decides: ὁ λόγος has it and is the subject, which makes θεός the predicate. Not “a god” — Greek can be perfectly definite with no article.

examples.english: for *he himself* is our peace
examples.note: αὐτός is a pronoun, so it wins — even though ἡ εἰρήνη has the article.

cards.name: Apposition
cards.eli5: Same person, two stickers. “Andrew, Peter’s brother.” No “is” — just a second sticker.

formula.note: No verb anywhere.

cards.oneLine: Two nominatives side by side, no verb. The second renames the first.
cards.mnemonic: No verb, just a name tag.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A sticker slapped on the first word: “Andrew — HELLO MY NAME IS the brother of Simon Peter.” Nothing is claimed; he is just being identified.
cards.spotIt: Two nominatives, a pause between them, and no “is” anywhere.
cards.bookDef: Further explains the subject by clarification, description, or identification.
cards.watchOut: The only difference from a predicate nominative is the verb. Comma = label. “Is” = claim. And watch the chart: Rom 1:1 is filed here because δοῦλος explains Παῦλος, while the near-identical Titus 1:1 is filed under absolute because there the whole salutation stands alone.

examples.english: Andrew, *the brother* of Simon Peter
examples.note: ἀδελφός renames Andrew. Nothing is being claimed about him.

examples.english: Paul, *a servant* of Christ Jesus
examples.note: δοῦλος renames Paul.

examples.english: Ivan, *the student*, came to class.
examples.note: A name tag. Compare “Ivan is the student” — that one has a verb, so it is a claim.

cards.name: Nominative of Address
cards.eli5: “Hey, Dad!” You are talking TO him, not about him.
cards.oneLine: A nominative used to call out to someone.
cards.mnemonic: "Hey, you!" in a nominative coat.
cards.mnemonicWhy: He is being spoken to, not described. It looks like a subject and works like a shout.
cards.spotIt: Try an exclamation mark after it. “Husbands! — love your wives.” If that works, it is address.
cards.bookDef: Used in the place of a vocative in direct address.
cards.watchOut: A subject is talked about. An address is talked to. Same case, opposite direction.

examples.english: Have mercy on us, *Son of David*
examples.note: He is being called out to, not described. Nominative shape, vocative job.

examples.english: *Husbands*, love your wives
examples.note: Not a statement about husbands. A shout at them.

cards.name: Nominative of Appellation
cards.eli5: It is the name on his badge. Everyone says “Teacher”, so that became his name.
cards.gist: a title used as a name

formula.note: X stays nominative.

cards.oneLine: A title used as somebody's name, left in the nominative.
cards.mnemonic: The title is on the name badge — and badges don't decline.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Once “Teacher” is what people call him, it stops behaving like a word in a sentence and behaves like the name printed on a badge.
cards.spotIt: It is a title, it is what someone is called, and it stayed nominative when the sentence wanted an accusative.
cards.bookDef: Used in conjunction with an address or title where a case other than the nominative would be expected.
cards.watchOut: The easiest of the four. If a nominative is plainly a title-as-name, stop looking for something cleverer.

examples.greek: ὑμεῖς φωνεῖτέ με *ὁ διδάσκαλος* καὶ *ὁ κύριος*
examples.english: You call me *Teacher* and *Lord*
examples.note: φωνεῖτέ με wants an accusative after it. The titles stay nominative because they are the name.

cards.name: Nominative Absolute
cards.eli5: It is the title on the front of a book. It sits on top and joins nothing.
cards.oneLine: A nominative attached to nothing — a heading or a greeting.
cards.mnemonic: Absolute = the headline.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A headline floats above the page, tied to nothing. No verb, no clause, no rope.
cards.spotIt: Opening material — a title, a greeting, a list — with no verb to hook it to.
cards.bookDef: Grammatically independent use of the nominative in introductory material (such as titles, headings, salutations, or addresses).
cards.watchOut: No rope at all. If a pronoun later picks the word back up, it is hanging, not absolute.

examples.english: *The beginning* of the gospel of Jesus Christ
examples.note: ἀρχή is nominative and stands completely alone. Everything hanging off it is genitive.

examples.english: *Grace, mercy, peace* from God the Father
examples.note: All nominative, all opening material, all tied to nothing.

examples.english: *Paul*, a servant of God
examples.note: The whole salutation stands alone, and Παῦλος is the word left hanging. Compare Rom 1:1, where the same phrase is filed under apposition.

cards.name: Hanging Nominative
cards.eli5: You say the thing, then point back at it. “The good seed? THOSE are the king’s kids.”
cards.oneLine: A loose nominative that a pronoun picks up later.
cards.mnemonic: It hangs by a pronoun.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The pronoun downstream is the rope. Cut it and the word drops — which is exactly what an absolute never had.
cards.spotIt: Find the loose nominative, then look ahead for the pronoun standing in its place.
cards.bookDef: The logical rather than syntactical subject at the beginning of a sentence.
cards.watchOut: Absolute = no connection. Hanging = connected in sense, but not in grammar.

examples.greek: τὸ δὲ καλὸν *σπέρμα*, οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς βασιλείας
examples.english: and the good *seed* — these are the sons of the kingdom
examples.note: σπέρμα is left dangling, but οὗτοι (“these”) does its job in the main clause. That pronoun is the rope.

examples.greek: *ὁ νικῶν* ποιήσω αὐτὸν στῦλον ἐν τῷ ναῷ τοῦ θεοῦ μου
examples.english: *The one who conquers*, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God
examples.note: ὁ νικῶν is left dangling, and αὐτόν picks it up. That pronoun is the rope.

cards.name: Direct Address
cards.eli5: You call his name. “Lazarus, come out!” The name is just how you got him to look.

formula.note: The name is not the doer. It is who you are shouting at.

cards.oneLine: Naming the person or thing you are speaking to.
cards.mnemonic: Say the name, then say the thing.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The whole case is one move: get their attention, then tell them. With or without “the” in front — the chart allows both.
cards.spotIt: Somebody is being called by name or title, and that word is not doing any work in the sentence.
cards.bookDef: The use of the articular or non-articular vocative to designate the person or thing being addressed.
cards.watchOut: When a word does this job but is shaped like a nominative, the chart calls it nominative of address instead. Same job, different clothes.

examples.english: *Lazarus*, come out!
examples.note: He is being called, not described. That is the vocative’s only job.

cards.name: The Case of Limitation
cards.eli5: Doing-words need a fence. This builds it. The doing stops here.
cards.oneLine: The accusative fences the verb in — it says how far the action goes.
cards.mnemonic: The nominative crowns; the accusative fences.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Every use is a fence post: onto whom (object), how far (measure), in what way (manner), about what (respect).
cards.spotIt: Two families. Does it act like a noun, or like an adverb?

examples.ref: The whole chapter in one line
examples.english: One object with four twists — Echo, Two, Sub, Alias — then the MMR shot: Measure, Manner, Respect.
examples.note: Noun-like first, adverb-like second.

cards.name: Double Accusative — Object and Complement
cards.eli5: You call the thing a name. “He gave his life AS a ransom.” The word “as” slips right in.

formula.note: Both are accusative. The second one is not a second victim — it is a label.

cards.oneLine: Two accusatives, where the second says what the first is called or made.
cards.mnemonic: CADETS — C: complement, you Call it something.
cards.mnemonicWhy: One test, one word: put “as” between the two accusatives. “His life AS a ransom.” “You AS friends.” If “as” fits, the second one is the complement.
cards.spotIt: Two accusatives with no “and” between them, and “as” slips in: object + complement.
cards.bookDef: A verb requires more than one accusative object to complete the thought, taking either (1) a personal and impersonal object or (2) a direct and predicate object.
cards.watchOut: Not apposition. Apposition renames something by what it already is; a complement says what it is being called, made or given as — and there is a verb doing the calling.

examples.english: to give his *life* as a *ransom* for many
examples.note: life is the object, ransom is what it was given as. “As” slips right in.

examples.english: I no longer call *you* *servants* … but I have called *you* *friends*
examples.note: Same construction twice in one verse. You are the object; servants and friends are what you get called.

examples.english: who gave *himself* as *a ransom* for all
examples.note: himself is the object, ransom is the label.

cards.name: Accusative of Apposition
cards.eli5: Two stickers again, on the catcher. “They picked Stephen, a good man.”
cards.oneLine: A second accusative that renames the first. No verb between them.
cards.mnemonic: CADETS — A: alias, the name tag on the object.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The same sticker you met in the nominative, now stuck on the catcher.
cards.spotIt: Two accusatives, no verb between them, and the second answers “which one, exactly?”
cards.bookDef: Two accusatives are juxtaposed, both referring to the same person or thing, with the second accusative further specifying the first accusative.
cards.watchOut: Not a complement. Apposition has no verb doing the naming: the two words simply sit side by side and the second one says which one, exactly.

examples.english: they chose Stephen, *a man* full of faith
examples.note: Stephen is the object; “a man” renames him.

examples.english: he will shepherd my people, *Israel*
examples.note: Israel renames “my people”.

examples.english: and on a colt, *the foal* of a donkey
examples.note: υἱόν renames πῶλον. One animal, two names.

cards.name: Direct Object
cards.eli5: This is the catcher. “I hit Ivan.” Ivan got hit.
cards.oneLine: What the verb lands on. By far the most common one.
cards.mnemonic: CADETS — D: the verb throws, the object catches.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The plain one, and the trunk the other four grow off. Get this solid first.
cards.spotIt: After the verb, ask: whom? what?
cards.bookDef: Serves as the recipient of the action.
cards.watchOut: A few verbs take their object in the genitive or the dative instead — ἀκούω, κρατέω, προσκυνέω. The case follows the verb, not the meaning.

examples.english: I hit *Ivan*.
examples.note: Ivan catches the hitting.

examples.greek: οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς *τὸν κόσμον*
examples.english: For God so loved *the world*
examples.note: The world is what the loving lands on.

examples.english: he saw *Simon*
examples.note: Ask the verb “whom?” and the accusative answers.

cards.name: Cognate Accusative
cards.eli5: The word says the doing-word again. “Sing a song.” “Fight a fight.”
cards.oneLine: An object that repeats the verb — same root, or same idea.
cards.mnemonic: CADETS — E: echo, the object repeats the verb.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Say the verb and hear it come straight back: sing a song, fight a fight, shepherd a flock.
cards.spotIt: Say the verb and the object out loud. Sounds redundant in English? Cognate.
cards.bookDef: Aligned with the verb either with regard to the lexical root or the idea conveyed.
cards.watchOut: Still the direct object. “Cognate” only names the flavour.

examples.english: fight *the good fight*
examples.note: The same root twice — the tightest echo there is.

examples.english: they rejoiced *with great joy* exceedingly
examples.note: ἐχάρησαν and χαράν are the same root. The echo is the whole point — it turns the volume up.

examples.english: I shepherd *a flock*.
examples.note: Not the same root, but the same idea. That counts too.

examples.english: I sing *a song*.
examples.note: The textbook one.

cards.name: Double Accusative — Person and Thing
cards.eli5: Two catchers, and one of them is a person. “Ask Dad for bread.” Dad and bread both catch it.

formula.note: Both are accusative. Neither one is a label — they are two real objects.

cards.oneLine: Two accusatives: somebody, and the thing done to them.
cards.mnemonic: CADETS — T: two catchers, a person and a thing.
cards.mnemonicWhy: You ASK a person FOR a thing. You TEACH a person A LESSON. Two objects, and “as” will not go between them — “asks him as bread” is nonsense.
cards.spotIt: Two accusatives, one of them a person, and “as” will not fit between them.
cards.bookDef: A verb requires more than one accusative object to complete the thought, taking either (1) a personal and impersonal object or (2) a direct and predicate object.
cards.watchOut: The usual verbs are asking, teaching, reminding, clothing and anointing — verbs that naturally take somebody and something.

examples.english: if his son asks *him* for *bread*
examples.note: him (a person) + bread (a thing). “Asks him as bread” is nonsense, so it is not a complement.

examples.english: he will teach *you* *all things*
examples.note: you (person) + all things (thing). Teaching verbs do this constantly.

examples.english: They taught *the class* *Greek*.
examples.note: Two objects, no label. The class is not “being called” Greek.

cards.name: Accusative Subject of the Infinitive
cards.eli5: Usually this one catches the ball. Not here — here it throws. “I want HIM to go.” He is the one going.

formula.note: X is accusative — and X is the one doing it.

cards.oneLine: An infinitive's subject is accusative, not nominative.
cards.mnemonic: CADETS — S: sub, the infinitive's own subject.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The odd one out — this accusative is doing the action, not catching it.
cards.spotIt: Find the infinitive, then the accusative that is doing it rather than receiving it.
cards.bookDef: Functions as the subject of an infinitive, indicating the agent performing the action conveyed by the infinitive.
cards.watchOut: The only accusative you translate as the doer — and only when there is an infinitive for it to be the subject of. No infinitive, no sub.

examples.english: …for *him* to go away
examples.note: “Him” is the one going. In Greek that word is accusative.

examples.greek: πρὸ τοῦ σε *Φίλιππον* φωνῆσαι … εἶδόν σε
examples.english: Before *Philip* called you … I saw you
examples.note: φωνῆσαι is the infinitive, and Philip is the one doing the calling — accusative, but the doer.

examples.english: he presented *himself* alive
examples.note: Careful — this one is a plain object, not a subject. There is no infinitive for it to be the subject of.

cards.name: Accusative of Measure
cards.eli5: How far? How long? “He walked a little bit.”
cards.oneLine: How far, how long, how much.
cards.mnemonic: MMR, shot one: How far?
cards.mnemonicWhy: The MMR shot, one of three. This is the one with a tape measure on it.
cards.spotIt: Ask: how far? how long? Does the accusative answer?
cards.bookDef: Functions in essence like an adverb in that it specifies measure (time or space).

examples.greek: καὶ προσελθὼν *μικρόν*, ἔπεσεν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ
examples.english: And going *a little farther* he fell on his face
examples.note: μικρόν measures the distance. It is not the object of anything.

cards.name: Accusative of Manner
cards.eli5: How did you do it? “He gave it for free.”
cards.oneLine: How the action is done.
cards.mnemonic: MMR, shot two: How?
cards.mnemonicWhy: The MMR shot, two of three. It turns a noun into an adverb: δωρεάν stops being “a gift” and becomes “freely”.
cards.spotIt: Ask: how? Check that an -ly word is the natural English.
cards.bookDef: Functions in essence like an adverb in that it specifies manner.

examples.english: being justified *freely* by his grace
examples.note: δωρεάν = freely, as a gift. It describes how the justifying happened.

cards.name: Accusative of Respect
cards.eli5: Only one part of you is meant. “Cut to the heart” — the heart is the part that hurt, not your skin.
cards.oneLine: In one way only — put “with respect to” in front of it.
cards.mnemonic: MMR, shot three: How so? — slot in "as to".
cards.mnemonicWhy: The MMR shot, three of three, and the narrowest fence. The verb happened, but only in one respect, and this names which.
cards.spotIt: Say it with “with respect to” in front. If that rescues the sense, this is it.
cards.bookDef: Restricts the reference of the verbal action, indicating in what regard an action is represented as true.
cards.watchOut: Easy to mistake for the object. If “with respect to” makes it better, it is respect.

examples.english: when they heard this they were pierced *to the heart*
examples.note: Not a surgical piercing but an inner one: the book spells the sense out as “pierced with reference to the heart”, and “with respect to” is what keeps it from sounding like an operation.

cards.name: Source
cards.eli5: It flowed out of that. “Righteousness of God” means righteousness FROM God.

formula.note: = that comes FROM X.

cards.oneLine: Where the head word came from.
cards.mnemonic: SWAMP RD — S: where it came from.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Swap “of” for “from” and see whether it still works. “The righteousness from God.”
cards.spotIt: Try “from” in place of “of”. Still makes sense? Source.
cards.bookDef: Indicates the origin of the head noun (“from”).
cards.watchOut: Separation also translates “from”. Source is where a noun came from; separation is what a verb moves away from.

examples.english: the righteousness *of God*
examples.note: The righteousness comes from God. Swap in “from” and it still reads.

cards.name: Partitive
cards.eli5: The “of” word is the big pile. The other word is your piece. “One of the boats.”

formula.note: The genitive is the WHOLE. The head noun is the part.

cards.oneLine: The genitive is the whole; the head word is a piece of it.
cards.mnemonic: SWAMP RD — W: the genitive is the whole pie, the head word your slice.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Backwards from what you expect: the word in the genitive is the bigger thing, not the smaller one.
cards.spotIt: Ask: is the genitive word the whole that the other word is a piece of?
cards.bookDef: Whether by itself or in conjunction with the preposition ἀπό or ἐκ, the articular noun in the genitive denotes the whole of which the head noun is a part.
cards.watchOut: Often turns up with ἀπό or ἐκ, and the genitive noun carries the article.

examples.english: one *of the boats*
examples.note: The boats are the whole; the one boat is the part.

cards.name: Attributive
cards.eli5: “The word of his power” really means “his POWERFUL word.” Squish it into a describing word.

formula.note: → his POWERFUL word. X becomes the adjective.

cards.oneLine: A quality of the head word — it could have been an adjective.
cards.mnemonic: SWAMP RD — A: turn the genitive into an adjective.
cards.mnemonicWhy: “The word of his power” → “his powerful word.” If the genitive can become the adjective, and saying it that way is stronger, it is attributive.
cards.spotIt: Try rewriting the genitive as an adjective in front of the head noun. Does it work?
cards.bookDef: Denotes an attribute or innate quality of the head term, conveying an emphatic adjectival idea.
cards.watchOut: Description is the vaguer cousin. Attributive earns its name because the genitive really does become an adjective.

examples.english: by his *powerful* word
examples.note: “Word of power” becomes “powerful word”. That rewrite is the test.

cards.name: Material or Content
cards.eli5: What it is made of, or what is in it. “A cup of water” is full of water.
cards.gist: Made of it, full of it

formula.note: = made of X, or full of X.

cards.oneLine: What it is made of, or what is inside it.
cards.mnemonic: SWAMP RD — M: made of it, or full of it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Cargo of gold is made of gold. A cup of water is full of water. One case, two flavours.
cards.spotIt: Ask: made of what? or full of what?
cards.bookDef: Indicates the material of which the head term is made or specifies the content of an object or abstract noun.

examples.english: cargo *of gold*
examples.note: Material — the cargo is made of gold.

examples.english: a cup *of water*
examples.note: Content — the cup is full of water.

cards.name: Possession
cards.eli5: It is his. “The house of Philip” means Philip’s house.

formula.note: = X’s. Try the apostrophe-s.

cards.oneLine: It belongs to X.
cards.mnemonic: SWAMP RD — P: whose? Try the apostrophe-s.
cards.mnemonicWhy: “The house of Philip” → “Philip’s house.” If the apostrophe-s works and means he owns it, it is possession.
cards.spotIt: Rewrite it with ’s. Does it mean he owns the thing?
cards.bookDef: Identifies ownership with regard to the noun it modifies, often employing the use of a possessive pronoun.
cards.watchOut: Relationship takes an apostrophe-s too — “Zebedee’s son”. Owning a thing is possession; family is relationship.

examples.english: we entered the house *of Philip*
examples.note: Philip’s house. He owns it.

cards.name: Relationship
cards.eli5: It is family, and Greek left the family word out. “James of Zebedee” means Zebedee’s son.

formula.note: → James, the SON of Zebedee. The kin word is missing.

cards.oneLine: X’s son, wife or parent — with the family word left out.
cards.mnemonic: SWAMP RD — R: supply the missing kin word.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Greek leaves out “son” or “wife” and expects you to know. Ἰάκωβον τὸν τοῦ Ζεβεδαίου is “James the [son] of Zebedee.”
cards.spotIt: A name in the genitive with no thing to own? Try slotting in “son of” or “wife of”.
cards.bookDef: Denotes a family relationship such as a person’s parent or spouse. The word indicating the relationship is often omitted and must be inferred.
cards.watchOut: Possession is owning a thing. Relationship is family, with the kin word usually left out.

examples.english: James the son *of Zebedee*
examples.note: “Son” is nowhere in the Greek. You supply it.

cards.name: Description
cards.eli5: The leftovers bin. Nobody owns it, it is not made of it — it just describes.

formula.note: Nothing more specific fits.

cards.oneLine: It describes the head word, and nothing more specific fits.
cards.mnemonic: SWAMP RD — D: the ditch at the end of the road.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Walk the ladder first. When nothing more specific fits, this catches it. A baptism of repentance is not owned by repentance, not made of it — just described by it.
cards.spotIt: Run the ladder. If no other category fits, it is description.
cards.bookDef: Further limits or describes the head noun, but other common genitival categories do not capture the specific nuance.
cards.watchOut: Do not reach for this first. It is the bottom of the ladder, not the top.

examples.english: a baptism *of repentance*
examples.note: Not possessed, not made of, not from. Just described.

cards.name: Subjective
cards.eli5: The “of” word is doing it. “The love of Christ” — Christ is doing the loving.

formula.note: → Christ loves. X does the action.

cards.oneLine: X is doing the action hidden in the head word.
cards.mnemonic: Subject does it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Turn the head noun back into a verb. “The love of Christ” → Christ loves. X is the one doing it.
cards.spotIt: Make the head noun a verb, then ask: is X doing it?
cards.bookDef: Functions semantically as the subject of the verbal idea implied in the head noun, producing the action.

examples.greek: τίς ἡμᾶς χωρίσει ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγάπης *τοῦ Χριστοῦ*;
examples.english: Who can separate us from the love *of Christ*?
examples.note: Christ is the one loving. Make the noun a verb and X is doing it.

cards.name: Objective
cards.eli5: The “of” word is getting it. “Faith of God” means faith IN God.

formula.note: → you believe God. X receives the action.

cards.oneLine: X is receiving the action hidden in the head word.
cards.mnemonic: Object gets it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Same move, other direction. “Faith of God” means faith IN God — God is on the receiving end.
cards.spotIt: Make the head noun a verb, then ask: is X getting it?
cards.bookDef: Functions semantically as the direct object of the verbal idea implicit in the head noun, receiving the action.
cards.watchOut: Subjective and objective look identical in Greek. Only the sense decides which one it is.

examples.english: Have faith *in God*
examples.note: God is believed in, not believing. X is receiving the action.

cards.name: Price
cards.eli5: How much did it cost? “Bought with a price.”

formula.note: for how much?

cards.oneLine: What it cost, or what it is worth.
cards.mnemonic: PACTS — P: for how much?
cards.mnemonicWhy: PACTS opens with the price, because the first thing any pact settles is what it costs. ἠγοράσθητε τιμῆς — you were bought at a price.
cards.spotIt: Ask: at what price? worth how much?
cards.bookDef: Indicates the price that is paid or the value that attaches to a given item.

examples.english: you have been bought *with a price*
examples.note: τιμῆς is what was paid.

cards.name: Means or Agency
cards.eli5: Who did it, or what did it. “Blessed BY my Father” — Dad did the blessing.

formula.note: by what? by whom?

cards.oneLine: By what, or by whom, the action was done.
cards.mnemonic: PACTS — A: by what? by whom?
cards.mnemonicWhy: A thing did it (means) or a person did it (agency). Both come out as “by”.
cards.spotIt: Ask: by what, or by whom? A thing = means. A person = agency.
cards.bookDef: Conveys the impersonal means or personal agent by which a given action is carried out (“by”).

examples.english: Since God is not tempted *by evil*
examples.note: Means — evil is a thing, not a person.

examples.english: Come, you who are blessed *by my Father*
examples.note: Agency — the Father is a person.

cards.name: Comparison
cards.eli5: This is the thing being beaten. “God is greater THAN our heart” — the heart is what he beat.

formula.note: than what?

cards.oneLine: What something is being measured against.
cards.mnemonic: PACTS — C: than what?
cards.mnemonicWhy: Find a comparative — greater, better, more — and the genitive beside it is the thing being beaten.
cards.spotIt: See a comparative adjective? The genitive next to it is the “than”.
cards.bookDef: Used to denote comparison in conjunction with a comparative adjective (“than”).

examples.greek: μείζων ἐστὶν ὁ θεὸς *τῆς καρδίας* ἡμῶν
examples.english: God is greater *than our heart*
examples.note: μείζων is the comparative; the genitive is what he is greater than.

cards.name: Time or Place
cards.eli5: When it happened, or where. “He came AT NIGHT” — night is the when.

formula.note: when? where?

cards.oneLine: When or where the action happened.
cards.mnemonic: PACTS — T: when? where?
cards.mnemonicWhy: The one with a clock and a map on it. Note the focus is the kind of time, not a point on a clock.
cards.spotIt: Ask: when did it happen? where did it happen?
cards.bookDef: Indicates the location in time or space where an action occurs. The focus is on kind or quality.

examples.greek: ὁ ἐλθὼν πρὸς αὐτὸν *νυκτὸς* τὸ πρῶτον
examples.english: who had previously come to him *at night*
examples.note: Time — night is the kind of time it happened in.

examples.english: After the exile *to Babylon*
examples.note: Place — where the exile went.

cards.name: Separation
cards.eli5: Moving away. “They walked away from the faith.”

formula.note: away from what?

cards.oneLine: What the action moves away from.
cards.mnemonic: PACTS — S: away from what?
cards.mnemonicWhy: Movement away, real or figurative — walking away from a place, or away from the faith.
cards.spotIt: Ask: away from what? Does “from” fit?
cards.bookDef: Indicates motion away from or distance, whether literally or figuratively (“from”).
cards.watchOut: Source also translates “from”. Separation moves away from something; source is where a noun came from.

examples.english: some will depart *from the faith*
examples.note: Movement away from — figurative, but still away.

cards.name: Apposition
cards.eli5: Two stickers, third time. “Jeremiah the prophet.” One man, two names.

formula.note: X is another name for the head noun.

cards.oneLine: A second name for the head word.
cards.mnemonic: The name tag again — third case running.
cards.mnemonicWhy: You have met this in the nominative and the accusative. Same move: the second word renames the first.
cards.spotIt: Ask: is the genitive another name for the head noun? “Jeremiah, who is the prophet.” “The gift, which is the Holy Spirit.”
cards.bookDef: The genitive of apposition provides an alternate designation (simple) of a genitive head noun or provides an explanatory (epexegetical) restatement of a head noun in any case.
cards.watchOut: Simple: the head noun is genitive too. Epexegetical: the head noun can be any case.

examples.english: through Jeremiah *the prophet*
examples.note: Simple — the head noun Ἰερεμίου is itself genitive.

examples.english: the gift *of the Holy Spirit*
examples.note: Epexegetical — the gift IS the Spirit. The head noun here is accusative.

cards.name: Direct Object
cards.eli5: Some doing-words are picky. Hearing, wanting, sharing, bossing and leaving all want their catcher dressed like this.

formula.note: The verb wanted a genitive, not an accusative.

cards.oneLine: The object of a verb that wants the genitive instead of the accusative.
cards.mnemonic: Feel it, want it, share it, rule it, leave it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Six kinds of verb do this: sensation and emotion (feel it), volition (want it), sharing, ruling, separation (leave it). It is a habit of the verb, not a meaning.
cards.spotIt: A genitive sitting where you expected an accusative? Check the verb: sensing, feeling, wanting, sharing, ruling, separating?
cards.bookDef: Verbs of sensation, emotion or volition, sharing, ruling, or separation take their direct object in the genitive case (instead of the accusative case).
cards.watchOut: This one follows a VERB. The objective genitive follows a NOUN.

examples.english: you did not lack *anything*, did you?
examples.note: ὑστερέω takes its object in the genitive.

examples.greek: οἱ νεκροὶ ἀκούσουσιν *τῆς φωνῆς* τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ
examples.english: the dead will hear *the voice* of the Son of God
examples.note: Sensation — hearing. Feel it.

examples.english: I have not coveted anyone’s *silver* or *gold* or *clothing*
examples.note: Emotion and volition — coveting. Want it.

examples.english: You cannot share in the Lord’s *table*
examples.note: Sharing. Share it.

examples.english: For sin will not rule over *you*
examples.note: Ruling. Rule it.

cards.name: Personal Interest
cards.eli5: Someone gains, or someone loses. “A bride dressed up FOR her husband.” “She had it IN for him.”

formula.note: Good for X, or bad for X.

cards.oneLine: Who benefits, or who suffers.
cards.mnemonic: PORT — P: for him, or against him.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Two directions, one use. Rev 21:2 is for somebody; Mark 6:19 is against somebody.
cards.spotIt: Ask: does this help someone, or hurt someone?
cards.bookDef: Denotes the person (or rarely, the thing) to whose benefit or detriment a verbal action occurs.
cards.watchOut: The chapter is candid that this is not a clean line. Brooks and Winbery: “All datives of advantage or disadvantage are in fact indirect objects, and all indirect objects to a greater or lesser degree express advantage or disadvantage.” Porter adds that the label combines syntax with context — it has to be inferred from the passage rather than read off the form. Expect a judgement call, not a test.

examples.english: like a bride adorned *for her husband*
examples.note: Advantage — she is dressed for his benefit.

examples.english: So Herodias held a grudge *against him*
examples.note: Disadvantage — the grudge is to his cost.

examples.greek: ὥστε μαρτυρεῖτε *ἑαυτοῖς* ὅτι υἱοί ἐστε τῶν φονευσάντων τοὺς προφήτας
examples.english: So you testify *against yourselves* that you are descendants of those who murdered the prophets
examples.note: Disadvantage — the obverse of advantage. The testimony lands on them, and not in their favour.

examples.greek: ὁ ἰὸς αὐτῶν εἰς μαρτύριον *ὑμῖν* ἔσται
examples.english: their corrosion will be a witness *against you*
examples.note: Not “a witness to you” but “against you”. When the dative names who suffers, “against” is usually the word.

examples.greek: μὴ θησαυρίζετε *ὑμῖν* θησαυροὺς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
examples.english: Don't store up *for yourselves* treasures on earth
examples.note: Advantage. The storing up was meant to benefit them — “for” is the word that carries it.

examples.greek: ἵνα οἱ ζῶντες μηκέτι *ἑαυτοῖς* ζῶσιν ἀλλὰ *τῷ* ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν *ἀποθανόντι* καὶ *ἐγερθέντι*
examples.english: so that those who live should no longer live *for themselves*, but *for the one who died* for them and was raised
examples.note: Two advantages set against each other in one clause: no longer for yourselves, but for him.

cards.name: Possession
cards.eli5: It is theirs, said backwards. “To you is the promise” means “you have the promise.”

formula.note: = X has it.

cards.oneLine: The dative owns the subject of a to-be verb.
cards.mnemonic: PORT — O: owns it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Greek says “to me is a book” where we say “I have a book”. Flip it round and the owner appears.
cards.spotIt: A dative sitting next to εἰμί or γίνομαι? Try flipping it into “X has”.
cards.bookDef: Unique construction in which the dative possesses the subject of an equative verb (such as εἰμι or γίνομαι).
cards.watchOut: It needs an equative verb — εἰμί, γίνομαι, ὑπάρχω — and the dative owns that verb's subject. Dana and Mantey call it “personal interest particularized to the point of ownership”. Against the genitive of possession the emphasis flips: the genitive stresses the person who owns, the dative stresses the thing owned.

examples.english: For the promise is *for you*
examples.note: “To you is the promise” = you have the promise.

examples.english: What is *your* name?
examples.note: More literally, “what name is to you?” The dative owns the subject of ἐστιν.

examples.english: *they* don't have a storeroom or a barn
examples.note: Literally “to them there is not a storeroom”. English turns the dative into the subject; Greek does not.

examples.english: *You have* a custom
examples.note: Literally “there is a custom to you”. Flip it round and the owner appears.

examples.greek: *ᾧ* ἐστιν ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων
examples.english: *To him* be the glory and the power forever and ever
examples.note: A doxology built on the same construction: the glory is the subject, and the dative owns it.

cards.name: Reference or Respect
cards.eli5: Only true about one thing. “He died TO SIN” — dead as far as sin goes, not dead all over.

formula.note: = with reference to X.

cards.oneLine: The one respect in which the statement holds.
cards.mnemonic: PORT — R: re:, like the subject line of an email.
cards.mnemonicWhy: “Re: sin — he died.” The dative names what the sentence is about, and the claim is only true about that. Robertson's rule of thumb for the whole pure dative: applied to a person it comes out as interest, applied to a thing it usually comes out as reference.
cards.spotIt: Put “with reference to” in front. Does the sentence stop being odd?
cards.bookDef: Limits the extent to which something is presented as true, qualifying a statement that would otherwise not be true.
cards.watchOut: The accusative has a respect use too (Acts 2:37, “cut with respect to the heart”) — same job, different case. This one also travels under a pile of other names: dative of respect, frame of reference dative, limiting dative, qualifying dative, contextualizing dative.

examples.english: he died *to sin* once for all
examples.note: Not dead altogether — dead with reference to sin.

examples.greek: οἱ κατεσθίοντες τὰς οἰκίας τῶν χηρῶν καὶ *προφάσει* μακρὰ προσευχόμενοι
examples.english: they devour widows' houses and say long prayers *just for show*
examples.note: With reference to appearance. The prayers are long only in that one respect.

examples.greek: πάντα τὰ γεγραμμένα διὰ τῶν προφητῶν *τῷ υἱῷ* τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
examples.english: everything written by the prophets *about the Son* of Man (ESV)
examples.note: “About” is the giveaway: the writing is with reference to him, not given to him.

examples.english: Everything is permissible *for me*
examples.note: With reference to me. It sets the boundary of the claim — permissible in my case.

examples.english: Even if I am untrained *in public speaking*
examples.note: Untrained in one respect only. Paul limits the admission to speech and no further.

cards.name: Indirect Object
cards.eli5: Who you gave it to. “Give glory to God.” God is the one getting it.

formula.note: The one who receives it.

cards.oneLine: The one to whom, or for whom, the act is done.
cards.mnemonic: PORT — T: to whom. The plain one.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The commonest dative there is, and the one English already taught you: you give it TO someone.
cards.spotIt: A giving or telling verb, a direct object, and a dative — that dative is the receiver.
cards.bookDef: Indicates the one for whom or in whose interest an act is performed.
cards.watchOut: Personal interest is widely treated as a specialised use of this one, so a dative that clearly benefits or harms someone can be labelled either way. Where the sentence hands something over and says nothing about gain or loss, indirect object is the safe answer.

examples.english: Give glory *to God*
examples.note: Glory is what is given; God is who it goes to.

examples.english: Then he told *them* many things in parables
examples.note: A telling verb, an accusative object (πολλά) and a dative — and the dative is who received the telling.

examples.greek: καὶ ἐλάλησαν *αὐτῷ* τὸν λόγον τοῦ κυρίου
examples.english: Then they spoke the word of the Lord *to him*
examples.note: Same shape again: τὸν λόγον is what was spoken, αὐτῷ is who it was spoken to.

examples.greek: ταύτην τὴν παραγγελίαν παρατίθεμαί *σοι*, τέκνον Τιμόθεε
examples.english: This charge I entrust *to you*, Timothy, my child (ESV)
examples.note: Paul entrusts the charge — the direct object — to Timothy, the indirect object.

examples.greek: οἱ πάσχοντες κατὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ *πιστῷ κτίστῃ* παρατιθέσθωσαν τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν
examples.english: let those who suffer according to God's will entrust themselves *to a faithful Creator*
examples.note: The same verb as 1 Tim 1:18, and the dative is personal again: it names the one the trust is placed in.

cards.name: Place
cards.eli5: Where it literally is. “Sitting in a circle.”

formula.note: A real spot you could point at.

cards.oneLine: The literal physical location.
cards.mnemonic: HIT — H: here, a real spot.
cards.mnemonicWhy: If you could stand there, it is place. If you could not, it is sphere.
cards.spotIt: Ask: could I actually point at this location?
cards.bookDef: Pinpoints the literal physical location of a noun in the dative case.
cards.watchOut: Greek leaves it a bare dative and English has to choose the preposition — in, on, among, at, to or by. Picking the wrong one is what makes a place dative look like means.

examples.english: those sitting *in a circle* around him
examples.note: A real ring of people on real ground.

examples.english: he took a sponge … put it *on a stick*, and offered him a drink
examples.note: Not “to or for a stick”, and not “by means of a stick” — on a stick. A physical location.

examples.greek: πλέξαντες στέφανον ἐξ ἀκανθῶν ἐπέθηκαν αὐτοῦ *τῇ κεφαλῇ*
examples.english: they twisted a crown of thorns and put it *on* his *head*
examples.note: A literal head. You could point at it, so it is place and not sphere.

examples.greek: τοῦτον ὁ θεὸς ἀρχηγὸν καὶ σωτῆρα ὕψωσεν *τῇ δεξιᾷ* αὐτοῦ
examples.english: God exalted this man *to his right hand* as ruler and Savior
examples.note: The chapter files this under place — exalted to a position. Some read it as means, “by his right hand”, so it is worth knowing both are on the table.

examples.english: those who serve *at the altar* (ESV)
examples.note: Where the serving happened. Note the English preposition changes — in, on, among, at, to, by — while the Greek stays a bare dative.

cards.name: Sphere
cards.eli5: Where it is, but not really. “Sighing deeply in his spirit” — you cannot point at that.
cards.gist: In a realm, not a spot

formula.note: A place you cannot point at.

cards.oneLine: The figurative realm the action happens in.
cards.mnemonic: HIT — I: in what realm.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Place is a spot on a map. Sphere is a spot you can only imagine — in the spirit, in the flesh, in Christ.
cards.spotIt: It reads like a location, but nobody could stand there.
cards.bookDef: Identifies the figurative or metaphorical location (i.e., sphere or realm) of a noun in the dative case.
cards.watchOut: Place and sphere are one word doing literal and figurative duty, and the test is whether you could point at it. Two further warnings from the chapter: some grammarians fold sphere into “dative of place” altogether, and some examples filed under sphere really belong under reference.

examples.english: sighing deeply *in* his *spirit*
examples.note: A realm, not a room.

examples.english: they are darkened *in their understanding*
examples.note: Understanding is not a place you could stand. The darkness is bounded logically, not spatially.

examples.greek: καὶ Μωϋσῆς μὲν πιστὸς ἐν *ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ* αὐτοῦ
examples.english: Moses was faithful as a servant *in all* God's *household*
examples.note: A household here is a sphere of belonging rather than a building, even with ἐν written in front of it.

examples.english: they always go astray *in their heart* (ESV)
examples.note: The heart is the realm the straying happens in. Nobody wanders about inside an actual heart.

examples.english: being put to death *in the flesh* but made alive *in the spirit*
examples.note: Two spheres set against each other in one line. Neither is a location you could visit.

cards.name: Time
cards.eli5: When it happened. “On the third day.”

formula.note: A point in time, not a stretch.

cards.oneLine: The point in time at which it happened.
cards.mnemonic: HIT — T: then.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Location again, but on a calendar instead of a map. A moment, not a duration.
cards.spotIt: Ask: when? And check it is a moment rather than a length of time.
cards.bookDef: Indicates the point in time (location in time) at which the action of a verb is accomplished.
cards.watchOut: Luke 23:56b–24:1a puts all three in one sentence: καὶ τὸ μὲν σάββατον ἡσύχασαν — accusative, how long they rested; τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων — dative, the day they came; ὄρθρου βαθέως — genitive, what kind of hour. Learn that one verse and the three cases of time are done.

examples.greek: καὶ *τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τρίτῃ* γάμος ἐγένετο
examples.english: *On the third day*, a wedding took place
examples.note: A point on the calendar.

examples.greek: ἐπορεύθη ὁ Ἰησοῦς *τοῖς σάββασιν* διὰ τῶν σπορίμων
examples.english: Jesus passed through the grainfields *on the Sabbath*
examples.note: The point in time at which he passed through — not how long it took.

examples.greek: καὶ *αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ* ἐπιστᾶσα ἀνθωμολογεῖτο τῷ θεῷ
examples.english: *At that very moment* she came up and began to thank God
examples.note: A moment, as sharp as the dative of time ever gets.

examples.greek: *τῇ νυκτὶ ἐκείνῃ* ἦν ὁ Πέτρος κοιμώμενος
examples.english: *on that very night* Peter was sleeping
examples.note: A night can be a stretch, but here it pins down which night. Point, not duration.

examples.greek: καὶ ἔπεσαν *μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ* εἴκοσι τρεῖς χιλιάδες
examples.english: and *in a single day* twenty-three thousand people died
examples.note: One day named as the point it happened on. Had the stress been on how long it lasted, Greek would reach for the accusative.

cards.name: Means
cards.eli5: The thing you used. “Cutting himself with stones.” The stones did not choose to.

formula.note: A thing, not a person.

cards.oneLine: The impersonal thing the action was done with.
cards.mnemonic: MAMA — M: means, the tool.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A tool has no will of its own. If the dative could have refused, it is agency, not means.
cards.spotIt: Ask: with what? And check the answer is a thing.
cards.bookDef: Denotes the impersonal means by which the action of a given verb is accomplished.
cards.watchOut: Brooks and Winbery call this the most common, the simplest and the most obvious use of the instrumental case, so it is the one to try first. The rule that settles it against agency: means is always impersonal.

examples.english: cutting himself *with stones*
examples.note: Stones are a tool. They did not decide anything.

examples.greek: ὥσπερ οὖν συλλέγεται τὰ ζιζάνια καὶ *πυρὶ* κατακαίεται
examples.english: just as the weeds are gathered and burned *with fire* (ESV)
examples.note: Fire is the instrument, and fire has no will. Impersonal, so means rather than agency.

examples.greek: *τοῖς δάκρυσιν* ἤρξατο βρέχειν τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ καὶ *ταῖς θριξὶν* … ἐξέμασσεν
examples.english: she began to wet his feet *with her tears* and wiped them *with the hair* of her head (ESV)
examples.note: Two instruments in one sentence. She is the agent; the tears and the hair are what she used.

examples.greek: ἀνεῖλεν δὲ Ἰάκωβον τὸν ἀδελφὸν Ἰωάννου *μαχαίρῃ*
examples.english: and he executed James, John's brother, *with the sword*
examples.note: The sword did not decide anything. Herod is the agent; the sword is the means.

examples.english: filled *with all unrighteousness, evil, greed, and wickedness*
examples.note: Four datives in a row, all means: what they are filled with.

cards.name: Agency
cards.eli5: The person who did it. “Led by the Spirit.”

formula.note: A person, not a thing.

cards.oneLine: The personal agent by whom the action was done.
cards.mnemonic: MAMA — A: agency, the doer.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Same “by”, but somebody chose it. Means is the hammer; agency is the carpenter.
cards.spotIt: Ask: by whom? And check the answer is a person.
cards.bookDef: Denotes the personal agency by which the action of a given verb is accomplished.
cards.watchOut: Means and agency are the same shape on the page, and the only test is whether the dative has a will. Two more tells: the verb is usually passive, and dative agency is uncommon — Greek normally says it with ὑπό and the genitive, so a bare dative agent is doing something unusual.

examples.english: But if you are led *by the Spirit*
examples.note: The Spirit chooses. That makes it agency.

examples.greek: προσέχετε … μὴ ποιεῖν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι *αὐτοῖς*
examples.english: be careful not to practise your righteousness in front of others, to be seen *by them*
examples.note: Passive verb, personal agent. That pair is the signature of agency.

examples.english: nothing deserving death has been done *by him* (ESV)
examples.note: Perfect passive, and the dative names who did it. A deed has a doer; a tool does not.

examples.english: a teacher of the Law, respected *by all the people* (NASB)
examples.note: The people are the ones doing the respecting, so they are the agent, not the means.

examples.english: seen *by angels*
examples.note: Short and easy to misread. Greek usually says agency with ὑπό and the genitive, so a bare dative agent is worth stopping over.

cards.name: Manner
cards.eli5: How you did it. “He spoke openly.”

formula.note: Turn it into an -ly word.

cards.oneLine: The style in which the action was done.
cards.mnemonic: MAMA — M: manner, the how.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Not what you used, but the style you did it in. If an -ly word is the natural English, this is it.
cards.spotIt: Ask: how? Check that an -ly adverb fits.
cards.bookDef: Denotes the manner in which the action of a given verb is accomplished.
cards.watchOut: Means answers “with what tool”. Manner answers “in what style”.

examples.english: He spoke *openly* about this
examples.note: Openly is a style, not a tool.

examples.english: and they conspired to arrest Jesus *in a treacherous way*
examples.note: Treachery is the style of the arrest, not the tool of it. Manner answers how.

examples.greek: ἐχάρη καὶ παρεκάλει πάντας *τῇ προθέσει* τῆς καρδίας προσμένειν τῷ κυρίῳ
examples.english: he encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord *with devoted hearts*
examples.note: How they were to remain: with purpose of heart. Note τῷ κυρίῳ in the same verse is the object of προσμένω.

examples.english: If I partake *with thankfulness* (ESV)
examples.note: Turn it into an adverb — thankfully — and manner is usually what you are holding.

examples.english: We all, *with unveiled faces*, are looking as in a mirror
examples.note: With unveiled face: the manner of the looking. A face is not the instrument you look with.

cards.name: Association
cards.eli5: Who came along. “Buried with him.” You went together.

formula.note: Alongside — not used as a tool.

cards.oneLine: The one the action is done alongside.
cards.mnemonic: MAMA — A: association, the company.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Also “with”, but company rather than tool. The verb often starts with συν-, which gives it away.
cards.spotIt: Ask: with whom, in the sense of together with? Look for a συν- verb.
cards.bookDef: Denotes the person or thing with which a person is associated or by which a person is accompanied.
cards.watchOut: Three uses come out as “with”: means (a tool), manner (a style), association (company).

examples.english: Having been buried *with him* in baptism
examples.note: συν- on the verb, and you were buried alongside him, not using him.

examples.greek: καὶ οὐκ ἠδύναντο *συν*τυχεῖν *αὐτῷ* διὰ τὸν ὄχλον
examples.english: they could not meet *with him* because of the crowd
examples.note: The συν- on the verb is what governs the dative. Spot the prefix and association is nearly always the answer.

examples.english: so that we could also reign *with you*
examples.note: συμβασιλεύω — reign together with. The σύν prefix again, assimilated to συμ- before the β.

examples.greek: ἐὰν δὲ καὶ χωρισθῇ, μενέτω ἄγαμος ἢ *τῷ ἀνδρὶ* καταλλαγήτω
examples.english: she must remain unmarried or be reconciled *to her husband*
examples.note: No σύν prefix on this one, but reconciling is a joining word and the husband is the party joined to.

examples.english: they were not united *with those who heard it* in faith
examples.note: συγκεράννυμι — mixed together with. τῇ πίστει sitting beside it is means, so one clause carries two dative jobs.

cards.name: Cause
cards.eli5: Why it happened. “I am dying of hunger.” Hunger is the reason.

formula.note: = because of X.

cards.oneLine: The reason or basis for the action.
cards.mnemonic: BEAD — B: because.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Slot “because of” in front and the sense holds. The reason can be outside you or inside you.
cards.spotIt: Ask: why? Then try “because of”.
cards.bookDef: Indicates the basis or reason of the action of a given verb, whether external (occasion) or internal (motivation).
cards.watchOut: Cause and means both come out as “by” in English. Wallace's line is the one to keep: means says how the action was performed, cause says what it was performed on the basis of.

examples.english: here I am dying [because] *of hunger*!
examples.note: Hunger is the reason, not the tool.

examples.greek: τινὲς δὲ *τῇ συνηθείᾳ* ἕως ἄρτι τοῦ εἰδώλου ὡς εἰδωλόθυτον ἐσθίουσιν
examples.english: but some, *being accustomed* to the idol until now, eat food as if it were sacrificed to an idol (NASB)
examples.note: They eat that way because of what they are used to. The dative gives the basis, not the method.

examples.greek: μή πως τῇ περισσοτέρᾳ *λύπῃ* καταποθῇ ὁ τοιοῦτος
examples.english: otherwise he may be overwhelmed *by excessive grief*
examples.note: Grief is why he is overwhelmed, not a tool somebody used on him. Cause, not means.

examples.greek: μόνον ἵνα *τῷ σταυρῷ* τοῦ Χριστοῦ μὴ διώκωνται
examples.english: only to avoid being persecuted *for the cross* of Christ
examples.note: The cross is the reason for the persecution, not the instrument of it.

examples.greek: ὅσοι *φόβῳ* θανάτου διὰ παντὸς τοῦ ζῆν ἔνοχοι ἦσαν δουλείας
examples.english: those held in slavery all their lives *by the fear* of death
examples.note: Fear is the grounds of the slavery. Wallace's test: means answers how, cause answers on what basis.

cards.name: Cognate Dative
cards.eli5: The word says the doing-word again. “They were astounded with a great astoundment.”

formula.note: Same stem, said twice.

cards.oneLine: A dative built from the same stem as its verb.
cards.mnemonic: BEAD — E: echo, second case running.
cards.mnemonicWhy: You met the echo in the accusative. Greek doubles the word for force where English just says “utterly”.
cards.spotIt: Say the verb and the dative out loud. Same root, or same idea?
cards.bookDef: Use of a dative noun that is a cognate (of the same stem) to the verb it modifies either formally or conceptually.
cards.watchOut: Also called the Hebraic dative, because Hebrew builds the same doubling. Do not translate it twice — English wants one intensifying word: utterly, fervently, earnestly, strictly.

examples.english: they were *utterly* astounded
examples.note: ἐξέστησαν and ἐκστάσει are the same stem. English flattens it to “utterly”.

examples.greek: ὁ κακολογῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα *θανάτῳ* τελευτάτω
examples.english: Whoever reviles father or mother must *surely* die (ESV)
examples.note: θανάτῳ with τελευτάτω — death beside a dying verb. The echo comes out in English as an intensifier.

examples.greek: ὁ δὲ φίλος τοῦ νυμφίου … *χαρᾷ* χαίρει
examples.english: the groom's friend … *rejoices greatly*
examples.note: χαρᾷ χαίρει: joy beside a rejoicing verb. Same root twice, and the effect is intensity, not repetition.

examples.greek: *παραγγελίᾳ* παρηγγείλαμεν ὑμῖν μὴ διδάσκειν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι τούτῳ
examples.english: We *strictly* charged you not to teach in this name (ESV)
examples.note: A charge beside a charging verb. The ESV turns the doubling into the single word “strictly”.

examples.english: We have *strictly* bound ourselves (ESV)
examples.note: An oath beside an oath-verb. This is the one sometimes called the Hebraic dative, because Hebrew does the same.

cards.name: Apposition
cards.eli5: Two stickers, fourth time. “Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons.” One person, two names.

formula.note: Same person, second name.

cards.oneLine: A second dative renaming the first.
cards.mnemonic: BEAD — A: alias, fourth case running.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Nominative, accusative, genitive, dative — the name tag turns up in all four. Learn it once, keep it forever.
cards.spotIt: Two datives side by side, no verb between them, both pointing at the same thing.
cards.bookDef: Two related substantives refer to the same person or thing.
cards.watchOut: Strictly this is a fact about the syntax rather than about the dative case itself: the second word is dative only because the word it renames is. Nothing about the dative's own meaning is in play.

examples.english: by Beelzebul, *the ruler* of the demons
examples.note: ἄρχοντι renames Βεελζεβούλ.

examples.greek: εὐχαριστοῦμεν τῷ θεῷ *πατρὶ* τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ πάντοτε
examples.english: We always thank God, *the Father* of our Lord Jesus Christ
examples.note: Two datives side by side and the second renames the first: “the Father” says which God.

examples.english: to the only God, our *Savior*
examples.note: σωτῆρι renames θεῷ. No verb between them — the second dative just identifies the first more exactly.

examples.greek: πλησίον τοῦ χωρίου ὃ ἔδωκεν Ἰακὼβ Ἰωσὴφ [τῷ] *υἱῷ αὐτοῦ*
examples.english: near the property Jacob had given Joseph, *his son*
examples.note: “His son” renames Joseph. The dative here is doing nothing of its own; it is only matching the word it renames.

examples.greek: ἐγένετο δὲ ἡμέρας ἱκανὰς μεῖναι ἐν Ἰόππῃ παρά τινι Σίμωνι *βυρσεῖ*
examples.english: Peter stayed some time in Joppa with Simon, *a leather tanner*
examples.note: βυρσεῖ renames Σίμωνι — which Simon, exactly. The trade is the identifier.

cards.name: Direct Object
cards.eli5: Some doing-words want it dressed this way: trusting, obeying, serving, worshipping, thanking, following.

formula.note: The dative is the object.

cards.oneLine: The object of a verb that takes the dative instead of the accusative.
cards.mnemonic: BEAD — D: devoted verbs.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Look at the list — trusting, obeying, serving, worshipping, thanking, following. Every one is a verb of devotion. That is the whole category in one word.
cards.spotIt: A dative where you expected an accusative? Check whether the verb is one of devotion.
cards.bookDef: The dative occurs after certain verbs of trusting, obeying, serving, worshiping, thanksgiving, or following and functions as the direct object.
cards.watchOut: The genitive has a fussy-verb list too — feel it, want it, share it, rule it, leave it. The dative's list is devotion.

examples.english: We always thank *God*
examples.note: εὐχαριστέω takes its object in the dative.

examples.greek: οἱ δὲ εὐθέως ἀφέντες τὰ δίκτυα ἠκολούθησαν *αὐτῷ*
examples.english: Immediately they left their nets and followed *him*
examples.note: ἀκολουθέω is a following verb, and following verbs take their object in the dative.

examples.greek: ὁ ἄνεμος καὶ ἡ θάλασσα ὑπακούει *αὐτῷ*
examples.english: the wind and the sea obey *him*
examples.note: ὑπακούω is an obeying verb. English gives it a plain object; Greek gives it a dative.

examples.greek: αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τῷ μὲν νοῒ δουλεύω *νόμῳ* θεοῦ τῇ δὲ σαρκὶ *νόμῳ* ἁμαρτίας
examples.english: with my mind I serve *the law* of God, but with my flesh *the law* of sin
examples.note: δουλεύω is a serving verb, so both νόμῳ are its objects. Watch the other two datives in the same verse — τῷ νοΐ and τῇ σαρκί are means, not objects.

examples.english: Abraham believed *God* (ESV)
examples.note: πιστεύω is a trusting verb. “Believed God”, and the dative is what he believed.

cards.name: Articular
cards.eli5: It has its “the”. ὁ λόγος — the word, with the little word in front.

formula.note: The article is present. That is all the word means.

cards.oneLine: A noun with the article on it.
cards.mnemonic: Articular — the joint is there.
cards.mnemonicWhy: ἄρθρον is Greek for a joint, and it is also the Greek word for the article. Arthritis is a complaint about joints. Articular means the joint is in place — the article is there.
cards.spotIt: ὁ, ἡ, τό or one of their forms sitting in front of the noun.
cards.watchOut: The chart uses this word rather than defining it — “the articular or non-articular vocative”, “the articular noun in the genitive”. It assumes you already know it.

examples.english: In the beginning was *the* Word
examples.note: ὁ λόγος is articular — and in the same verse θεός is not, which is the whole argument.

examples.english: *salvation* is from the Jews
examples.note: Articular in Greek even though English drops the “the”.

cards.name: Anarthrous
cards.eli5: No “the” at all. λόγος standing on its own.

formula.note: The article is absent. That is all the word means — not what the absence implies.

cards.oneLine: A noun with no article on it.
cards.mnemonic: Anarthrous — ἀν- no, ἄρθρον joint. No joint, no article.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The same ἄρθρον, with the alpha privative bolted on the front — the same ἀν- that turns a theist into an atheist. No joint means no article.
cards.spotIt: A noun standing bare, with no ὁ, ἡ or τό in front of it.
cards.watchOut: Two things this word does not mean. It is not the chart's word — the chart says “the absence of the article”, so that is the phrasing an exam will use. And it never means “a”: what an absent article conveys is the three-way question under Poof.

examples.english: and the Word was *God*
examples.note: θεός is anarthrous. That is the fact; what it means is a separate question, and the answer is not “a god”.

examples.english: *Paul* and *Silas* were praying
examples.note: Anarthrous and still perfectly definite — a proper name needs no article.

cards.name: Monadic Article
cards.eli5: There is only one of him. “The only Son” — there is no second one to confuse him with.
cards.oneLine: The article on something one-of-a-kind.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — M: Monadic, the only one there is.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Not “the best of several” — there are no several. The sun, the devil, the only Son.
cards.spotIt: Ask whether a second one could even exist. If not, monadic.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.

examples.english: that he gave *his* only Son
examples.note: Monadic — there is only one of him.

cards.name: Abstract Article
cards.eli5: It points at the idea, not at one example of it. “Salvation” — the whole thing, not one rescue.
cards.oneLine: The article on an abstract noun, naming the concept.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — A: Abstract, the idea itself.
cards.mnemonicWhy: English usually drops the “the” here, which is why it is easy to miss: ἡ σωτηρία is just “salvation”.
cards.spotIt: An abstract noun with an article that English would not translate.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.

examples.english: *salvation* is from the Jews
examples.note: Abstract — the idea itself, not one instance of it.

cards.name: Generic Article
cards.eli5: It points at all of them at once. “Beware of false prophets” — the whole breed, not particular men.
cards.oneLine: The article on a class as a class, rather than on one member of it.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — G: Generic, all of them at once.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The one letter of MAGPIE that is not particularising. The chart's sentence has two halves — “particularizes … or uses it generically” — and this is the second half.
cards.spotIt: Swap in “that kind of thing” and see if it still works. If it does, generic.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.
cards.watchOut: This is the odd one out. The other five particularise; this one generalises.

examples.english: Be on your guard against *false prophets*
examples.note: Generic — the whole class of them, not particular ones.

cards.name: Par Excellence
cards.eli5: Not a prophet — THE Prophet. The one who deserves the name more than anyone.
cards.oneLine: The article marking the one that best deserves the title.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — P: Par excellence, the one worth the name.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Say it out loud with the stress on “the”. If “THE Prophet” sounds right, that is this one.
cards.spotIt: Try putting the stress on “the”. THE Christ, THE Prophet, THE day.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.
cards.watchOut: Close to monadic. Monadic means there is only one; par excellence means there are several and this is the one that counts.

examples.english: Are you *the* Prophet?
examples.note: Par excellence — not a prophet, THE prophet.

cards.name: Simple Identification
cards.eli5: It just picks out which one you mean. The plain job, and the commonest.
cards.oneLine: The article singling out one particular person or thing.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — I: Identification, this one here.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The default. If none of the other five fit, it is doing the plain job of saying which one.
cards.spotIt: Nothing clever going on — it just tells you which one is meant.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.

examples.greek: ποῦ ἐστιν *ὁ* τεχθεὶς βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων
examples.english: Where is *he* who has been born King of the Jews?
examples.note: Identification — it picks out one particular person.

cards.name: Anaphoric Article
cards.eli5: It means “that one, the one I just said”. The water he was talking about a moment ago.
cards.oneLine: The article pointing back at something already named.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — E: Earlier, the one already mentioned.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Translate it “that” instead of “the” and see if the sentence improves. If it does, it is anaphoric — and E is for Earlier, because the thing was named earlier.
cards.spotIt: Look backwards. Was this noun introduced a sentence or two ago without an article? Then this article is pointing at it.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.
cards.watchOut: The most common of the five in narrative, and the easiest to read straight past.

examples.greek: πόθεν οὖν ἔχεις *τὸ* ὕδωρ τὸ ζῶν
examples.english: So where do You get *that* ‘living water’?
examples.note: Anaphoric — the water already mentioned. Translate it “that”.

cards.name: Article as Personal Pronoun
cards.eli5: The article is the subject all by itself. “And they said to him.”
cards.oneLine: ὁ / οἱ standing alone as he, she or they — usually with δέ.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Personal: ὁ δέ means “and he”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: ὁ δέ and οἱ δέ are so common in narrative they are worth learning as a phrase: “and he …”, “and they …”.
cards.spotIt: An article with no noun, carrying δέ, at the head of a clause.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.english: *They* told him
examples.note: Personal — the article is the subject on its own.

cards.name: Article as Relative Pronoun
cards.eli5: The article starts a “who” clause. “Your Father who is in heaven.”
cards.oneLine: The article introducing a phrase that describes the noun before it.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Relative: the article that means “who”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: It is a chain link: the article hooks the phrase behind it onto the noun in front of it.
cards.spotIt: An article repeated after a noun, with a phrase rather than a noun after it.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.greek: τὸν πατέρα ὑμῶν *τὸν* ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς
examples.english: your Father *who* is in heaven
examples.note: Relative — the article introduces the clause.

cards.name: Article as Possessive Pronoun
cards.eli5: The article means “his”. Greek does not bother with αὐτοῦ when it is obvious.
cards.oneLine: The article doing the work of a possessive pronoun.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Possessive: the article that means “his”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: If the owner is obvious from the sentence, Greek leaves the possessive out and lets the article carry it. English has to put it back.
cards.spotIt: An article where English needs “his”, “her” or “their” and there is no genitive pronoun to supply it.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.english: And he divided *his* property between them
examples.note: Possessive — no αὐτοῦ needed, the article carries it.

cards.name: Article as Demonstrative Pronoun
cards.eli5: The article means “those”. “Those in the boat worshipped him.”
cards.oneLine: The article standing in for this, that, these or those.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Demonstrative: the article that means “those”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Usually with a phrase hanging off it: οἱ ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ — “those in the boat”.
cards.spotIt: An article with no noun, followed by a prepositional phrase.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.english: *those* in the boat worshiped him
examples.note: Demonstrative — “those”.

cards.name: Article as Alternate Pronoun
cards.eli5: Two articles taking turns. “Some as apostles… others as prophets.”
cards.oneLine: ὁ μέν … ὁ δέ, dividing a group into some and others.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Alternate: μέν … δέ, some … others.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The tell is the pair of little words. μέν sets up “on the one hand”, δέ answers “on the other”.
cards.spotIt: μέν on one article and δέ on another, splitting a list in two.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.english: He gave *some* as apostles
examples.note: Alternate — μέν … δέ, some … others.

cards.name: Absence — Indefinite
cards.eli5: No “the”, and it really does mean “a”. A boat. Any boat.
cards.oneLine: The missing article marking something non-particular: one of many.
cards.mnemonic: Poof — Indefinite: it really is “a”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: This is the reading everyone reaches for first, and it is right about a third of the time. Ask the other two before settling.
cards.spotIt: Would “a” or “some” read naturally? Then indefinite.
cards.bookDef: The absence of the article may convey that a given substantive is non-particular (indefinite or qualitative) or definite. If definite, this may be in conjunction with a proper name, a prepositional object, ordinal numbers, in predicate nominatives, as the complement in an object, complement construction, with monadic (one-of-a-kind) nouns, with abstract or generic nouns, with a pronominal adjective, or with technical expressions.

examples.english: to have *a small boat* ready for him
examples.note: Indefinite — genuinely “a”.

cards.name: Absence — Qualitative
cards.eli5: No “the”, and it is pointing at the quality itself. “Full of grace” — grace-ness, not a portion of grace.
cards.oneLine: The missing article stressing the nature of the thing rather than its identity.
cards.mnemonic: Poof — Qualitative: the stuff itself, not a piece of it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Also non-particular, like indefinite — but the emphasis is on what kind, not on which one. Add “the very nature of” in your head and see if it fits.
cards.spotIt: Would “the quality of” or “the very nature of” fit in front of it? Then qualitative.
