extraQuiz.why: Aorist active indicative, 3rd plural, ἀκολουθέω — perfective. Hearing and following are told as two whole steps; the ongoing speaking sits in the present participle λαλοῦντος.

extraQuiz.prompt: What he has seen and heard, to this he testifies, and no one receives his testimony
extraQuiz.greek: ὃ *ἑώρακεν* καὶ ἤκουσεν τοῦτο μαρτυρεῖ, καὶ τὴν μαρτυρίαν αὐτοῦ οὐδεὶς λαμβάνει (John 3:32)
extraQuiz.english: What he has seen and heard, to this he testifies, and no one receives his testimony
extraQuiz.why: Perfect active indicative, 3rd singular, ὁράω — stative. What he saw is a state he now stands in: he is an eyewitness.

extraQuiz.prompt: What he has seen and heard, to this he testifies, and no one receives his testimony
extraQuiz.greek: ὃ ἑώρακεν καὶ *ἤκουσεν* τοῦτο μαρτυρεῖ, καὶ τὴν μαρτυρίαν αὐτοῦ οὐδεὶς λαμβάνει (John 3:32)
extraQuiz.english: What he has seen and heard, to this he testifies, and no one receives his testimony
extraQuiz.why: Aorist active indicative, 3rd singular, ἀκούω — perfective. Side by side with the perfect ἑώρακεν: the hearing is told as an event, the seeing as a state.

extraQuiz.prompt: What he has seen and heard, to this he testifies, and no one receives his testimony
extraQuiz.greek: ὃ ἑώρακεν καὶ ἤκουσεν τοῦτο *μαρτυρεῖ*, καὶ τὴν μαρτυρίαν αὐτοῦ οὐδεὶς λαμβάνει (John 3:32)
extraQuiz.english: What he has seen and heard, to this he testifies, and no one receives his testimony
extraQuiz.why: Present active indicative, 3rd singular, μαρτυρέω — imperfective. The testifying is pictured as going on.

extraQuiz.prompt: He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ *ἥψατο* τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῆς, καὶ ἀφῆκεν αὐτὴν ὁ πυρετός, καὶ ἠγέρθη καὶ διηκόνει αὐτῷ (Matt 8:15)
extraQuiz.english: He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him
extraQuiz.why: Aorist middle indicative, 3rd singular, ἅπτομαι — perfective. A touch is punctual and telic, so the aorist is its default.

extraQuiz.prompt: He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ ἥψατο τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῆς, καὶ *ἀφῆκεν* αὐτὴν ὁ πυρετός, καὶ ἠγέρθη καὶ διηκόνει αὐτῷ (Matt 8:15)
extraQuiz.english: He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him
extraQuiz.why: Aorist active indicative, 3rd singular, ἀφίημι — perfective. The second of three aorists that carry the story forward.

extraQuiz.prompt: He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ ἥψατο τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῆς, καὶ ἀφῆκεν αὐτὴν ὁ πυρετός, καὶ *ἠγέρθη* καὶ διηκόνει αὐτῷ (Matt 8:15)
extraQuiz.english: He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him
extraQuiz.why: Aorist passive indicative, 3rd singular, ἐγείρω — perfective. Getting up is a bounded act, told whole.

extraQuiz.prompt: He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ ἥψατο τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῆς, καὶ ἀφῆκεν αὐτὴν ὁ πυρετός, καὶ ἠγέρθη καὶ *διηκόνει* αὐτῷ (Matt 8:15)
extraQuiz.english: He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him
extraQuiz.why: Imperfect active indicative, 3rd singular, διακονέω — imperfective. After three aorists, the story stops on an imperfect: her serving is pictured as going on (‘began to serve’).

extraQuiz.prompt: Then Jerusalem and all Judea were going out to him … and they were being baptised by him in the Jordan river
extraQuiz.greek: τότε *ἐξεπορεύετο* πρὸς αὐτὸν Ἱεροσόλυμα καὶ πᾶσα ἡ Ἰουδαία … καὶ ἐβαπτίζοντο ἐν τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ ποταμῷ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ (Matt 3:5–6)
extraQuiz.english: Then Jerusalem and all Judea were going out to him … and they were being baptised by him in the Jordan river
extraQuiz.why: Imperfect middle indicative, 3rd singular, ἐκπορεύομαι — imperfective. Crowd after crowd, pictured as a stream that kept coming. (The book prints Matt 3:5; ἐβαπτίζοντο is in 3:6 in the Greek text.)

extraQuiz.prompt: Then Jerusalem and all Judea were going out to him … and they were being baptised by him in the Jordan river
extraQuiz.greek: τότε ἐξεπορεύετο πρὸς αὐτὸν Ἱεροσόλυμα καὶ πᾶσα ἡ Ἰουδαία … καὶ *ἐβαπτίζοντο* ἐν τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ ποταμῷ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ (Matt 3:5–6)
extraQuiz.english: Then Jerusalem and all Judea were going out to him … and they were being baptised by him in the Jordan river
extraQuiz.why: Imperfect passive indicative, 3rd plural, βαπτίζω — imperfective. One baptism after another, pictured as going on.

extraQuiz.prompt: Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt
extraQuiz.greek: ἐγερθεὶς *παράλαβε* τὸ παιδίον καὶ τὴν μητέρα αὐτοῦ καὶ φεῦγε εἰς Αἴγυπτον (Matt 2:13)
extraQuiz.english: Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt
extraQuiz.why: Aorist active imperative, 2nd singular, παραλαμβάνω — perfective. Taking them is telic, and this is one specific night: the aorist is the default, not an emphasis.

extraQuiz.prompt: Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt
extraQuiz.greek: ἐγερθεὶς παράλαβε τὸ παιδίον καὶ τὴν μητέρα αὐτοῦ καὶ *φεῦγε* εἰς Αἴγυπτον (Matt 2:13)
extraQuiz.english: Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt
extraQuiz.why: Present active imperative, 2nd singular, φεύγω — imperfective. A verb of motion, which the chart says almost always comes in the present: lexical determination, so the default. It is not ‘keep fleeing’.

extraQuiz.prompt: Put your finger here and see my hands
extraQuiz.greek: φέρε τὸν δάκτυλόν σου ὧδε καὶ *ἴδε* τὰς χεῖράς μου (John 20:27)
extraQuiz.english: Put your finger here and see my hands
extraQuiz.why: Aorist imperative, 2nd singular, ὁράω (εἶδον) — perfective. The chart names ἴδε itself: it only comes aorist, so the form says nothing. (The book glosses it ‘aor mid impv’; the form is active.)

extraQuiz.prompt: and bring your hand and put it into my side
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ *φέρε* τὴν χεῖρά σου καὶ βάλε εἰς τὴν πλευράν μου (John 20:27)
extraQuiz.english: and bring your hand and put it into my side
extraQuiz.why: Present imperative, 2nd singular, φέρω — imperfective. A verb of carrying and motion whose imperative is nearly always present (φέρε, φέρετε): determination, the default. (The book glosses it ‘pres mid impv’; the form is active.)

extraQuiz.prompt: and bring your hand and put it into my side
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ φέρε τὴν χεῖρά σου καὶ *βάλε* εἰς τὴν πλευράν μου (John 20:27)
extraQuiz.english: and bring your hand and put it into my side
extraQuiz.why: Aorist imperative, 2nd singular, βάλλω — perfective. Putting the hand in is telic and for this one occasion: grammatical, and the default. Note φέρε (present) and βάλε (aorist) in the same breath — the difference is the verbs, not Jesus' emphasis. (The book glosses it ‘aor mid impv’; the form is active.)

extraQuiz.prompt: So they shouted, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!”
extraQuiz.greek: ἐκραύγασαν οὖν ἐκεῖνοι· *ἆρον* ἆρον, σταύρωσον αὐτόν (John 19:15)
extraQuiz.english: So they shouted, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!”
extraQuiz.why: Aorist active imperative, 2nd singular, αἴρω — perfective. A telic verb demanding one deed on one occasion: grammatical, the default. (It is also a command inside a narrative, which prefers the aorist too.)

extraQuiz.prompt: So they shouted, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!”
extraQuiz.greek: ἐκραύγασαν οὖν ἐκεῖνοι· ἆρον ἆρον, *σταύρωσον* αὐτόν (John 19:15)
extraQuiz.english: So they shouted, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!”
extraQuiz.why: Aorist active imperative, 2nd singular, σταυρόω — perfective. Crucifying is telic and this is one specific demand: the expected aorist.

extraQuiz.prompt: Put on then, as God's chosen ones … compassion, kindness, humility … bearing with one another
extraQuiz.greek: *ἐνδύσασθε* οὖν, ὡς ἐκλεκτοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ … σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ χρηστότητα ταπεινοφροσύνην … ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων (Col 3:12–13)
extraQuiz.english: Put on then, as God's chosen ones … compassion, kindness, humility … bearing with one another
extraQuiz.why: Aorist middle imperative, 2nd plural, ἐνδύω — perfective. Putting on clothes is telic, but this is a letter, where the present is preferred: the aorist is not the contextual default. It pictures the new character as put on, whole — the same verb as ἐνδυσάμενοι in 3:10.

extraQuiz.prompt: Put on then … compassion … bearing with one another and forgiving each other
extraQuiz.greek: ἐνδύσασθε οὖν … σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ … *ἀνεχόμενοι* ἀλλήλων καὶ χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς (Col 3:12–13)
extraQuiz.english: Put on then … compassion … bearing with one another and forgiving each other
extraQuiz.why: Present middle participle, nominative masculine plural, ἀνέχομαι — imperfective. Bearing with one another is atelic and ongoing: the present is the default.

extraQuiz.prompt: If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown out like a branch and withers
extraQuiz.greek: ἐὰν μή τις μένῃ ἐν ἐμοί, *ἐβλήθη* ἔξω ὡς τὸ κλῆμα καὶ ἐξηράνθη (John 15:6)
extraQuiz.english: If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown out like a branch and withers
extraQuiz.why: Aorist passive indicative, 3rd singular, βάλλω. A general rule about anyone who does not abide — gnomic. Arguable: some read it as futuristic (the end told as done).

extraQuiz.prompt: By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit
extraQuiz.greek: ἐν τούτῳ *ἐδοξάσθη* ὁ πατήρ μου, ἵνα καρπὸν πολὺν φέρητε (John 15:8)
extraQuiz.english: By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit
extraQuiz.why: Aorist passive indicative, 3rd singular, δοξάζω. A standing truth — whenever you bear fruit, the Father is glorified — gnomic. Arguable: futuristic is also defended.

extraQuiz.prompt: by him this man stands before you well
extraQuiz.greek: ἐν τούτῳ οὗτος *παρέστηκεν* ἐνώπιον ὑμῶν ὑγιής (Acts 4:10)
extraQuiz.english: by him this man stands before you well
extraQuiz.why: Perfect active indicative, 3rd singular, παρίστημι. ἕστηκα and its compounds mean ‘stand’: perfect form, present meaning — present state. Compare the pluperfect παρειστήκεισαν in Acts 1:10.

extraQuiz.prompt: Tychicus … whom I am sending to you
extraQuiz.greek: Τύχικος … ὃν *ἔπεμψα* πρὸς ὑμᾶς (Col 4:7–8)
extraQuiz.english: Tychicus … whom I am sending to you
extraQuiz.why: Aorist active indicative, 1st singular, πέμπω. Tychicus is carrying the letter: by the time they read it he has been sent — epistolary, translated ‘I am sending’.

extraQuiz.prompt: No one has ever seen God
extraQuiz.greek: θεὸν οὐδεὶς πώποτε *τεθέαται* (1 John 4:12)
extraQuiz.english: No one has ever seen God
extraQuiz.why: Perfect middle indicative, 3rd singular, θεάομαι. With πώποτε, ‘ever’, the stress is on the act never having happened — consummative, ‘has ever seen’. Arguable: intensive (no one stands as having seen him) is a fair reading.

extraQuiz.prompt: and they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ *ἔζησαν* καὶ ἐβασίλευσαν μετὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ χίλια ἔτη (Rev 20:4)
extraQuiz.english: and they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years
extraQuiz.why: Aorist active indicative, 3rd plural, ζάω. A verb of state in the aorist marking its start: they came to life — inceptive. (Constative ‘they lived’ is possible, but 20:5 speaks of the rest not coming to life.)

extraQuiz.prompt: and they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ ἔζησαν καὶ *ἐβασίλευσαν* μετὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ χίλια ἔτη (Rev 20:4)
extraQuiz.english: and they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years
extraQuiz.why: Aorist active indicative, 3rd plural, βασιλεύω. A thousand years of reigning in one aorist — the whole stretch seen at once, like Rom 5:14: constative.

extraQuiz.prompt: many false prophets have gone out into the world
extraQuiz.greek: πολλοὶ ψευδοπροφῆται *ἐξεληλύθασιν* εἰς τὸν κόσμον (1 John 4:1)
extraQuiz.english: many false prophets have gone out into the world
extraQuiz.why: Perfect active indicative, 3rd plural, ἐξέρχομαι. The point is the situation now: they are out there, which is why the readers must test the spirits — intensive. Arguable: consummative (‘have gone out’) is also read.

extraQuiz.prompt: behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside
extraQuiz.greek: ἰδοὺ ἡ μήτηρ καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ *εἱστήκεισαν* ἔξω (Matt 12:46)
extraQuiz.english: behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside
extraQuiz.why: Pluperfect active indicative, 3rd plural, ἵστημι. ἕστηκα means ‘stand’, so its pluperfect is a simple past state — ‘were standing’, with no earlier act in view. The same as Acts 1:10.

extraQuiz.prompt: A wife is bound as long as her husband lives
extraQuiz.greek: γυνὴ *δέδεται* ἐφ᾿ ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς (1 Cor 7:39)
extraQuiz.english: A wife is bound as long as her husband lives
extraQuiz.why: Perfect passive indicative, 3rd singular, δέω. A rule true of any wife — gnomic. Arguable: intensive (she stands bound) is close.

extraQuiz.prompt: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out
extraQuiz.greek: Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή, ἀφ᾿ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ *ἐξεληλύθει* (Luke 8:2)
extraQuiz.english: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out
extraQuiz.why: Pluperfect active indicative, 3rd singular, ἐξέρχομαι. Before the story, the demons had already gone out of her: the completion of a past action — consummative. Arguable: intensive (she was a woman set free) is possible.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the accusative, “each, in turn, up”.
extraQuiz.why: ἀνά — “each, in turn, up”. 13 times in the GNT. Anabaptists baptised again — ἀνά is “up”, “again”, “each in turn”. Only thirteen times in the NT, so recognise it and move on.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the genitive, “in place of, instead of”.
extraQuiz.why: ἀντί — “in place of, instead of”. 22 times in the GNT. An ANTI-christ is one who sets himself up in place of Christ. ἀντί is substitution: a ransom ἀντὶ πολλῶν, “in place of many”.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the genitive, “from, of”.
extraQuiz.why: ἀπό — “from, of”. 646 times in the GNT. APOstasy is falling away from; an APOstle is sent from. ἀπό is away from the edge of something.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the accusative, “into, in, at”.
extraQuiz.why: εἰς — “into, in, at”. 1768 times in the GNT. Into. The accusative is the case of direction, and εἰς is the most accusative word there is: motion into.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the genitive, “from, out of”.
extraQuiz.why: ἐκ — “from, out of”. 914 times in the GNT. EXit — ἐκ (ἐξ before a vowel) is out of from the inside. ἀπό leaves from the edge; ἐκ comes out from within.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the dative, “in, into, by”.
extraQuiz.why: ἐν — “in, into, by”. 2752 times in the GNT. IN. The commonest preposition in the NT, and it only ever takes the dative — the case of place, of being in something.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the genitive, “before, at”.
extraQuiz.why: πρό — “before, at”. 47 times in the GNT. PROlogue, the word before; PROphet, one who speaks before. πρό is before, in time or place.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the dative, “with”.
extraQuiz.why: σύν — “with”. 128 times in the GNT. SYNagogue, where people gather with; SYNoptic, seeing with. σύν is together with, and dative like the dative of association.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “through”; + accusative “because of”.
extraQuiz.why: διά — διά takes 2 cases — + genitive “through”; + accusative “because of”. 667 times in the GNT. DIAmeter goes through the circle. With the genitive, through; with the accusative, because of — the reason you went through.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “against”; + accusative “according to”.
extraQuiz.why: κατά — κατά takes 2 cases — + genitive “against”; + accusative “according to”. 473 times in the GNT. CATAstrophe comes down against you. With the genitive, against; with the accusative, according to — the gospel κατὰ Μαθθαῖον.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “with”; + accusative “after”.
extraQuiz.why: μετά — μετά takes 2 cases — + genitive “with”; + accusative “after”. 469 times in the GNT. METAphysics was the book shelved after the Physics. With the genitive, with (in company); with the accusative, after.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “concerning”; + accusative “around”.
extraQuiz.why: περί — περί takes 2 cases — + genitive “concerning”; + accusative “around”. 333 times in the GNT. PERImeter goes around. With the accusative, around; with the genitive, concerning — talk that goes round a subject.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “for”; + accusative “above”.
extraQuiz.why: ὑπέρ — ὑπέρ takes 2 cases — + genitive “for”; + accusative “above”. 150 times in the GNT. HYPER is over and above. With the accusative, above; with the genitive, for — on behalf of, standing over someone to shield them.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “by”; + accusative “under”.
extraQuiz.why: ὑπό — ὑπό takes 2 cases — + genitive “by”; + accusative “under”. 220 times in the GNT. HYPOdermic goes under the skin. With the accusative, under; with the genitive, by — the agent behind a passive verb.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “on, upon”; + dative “upon”; + accusative “against”.
extraQuiz.why: ἐπί — ἐπί takes 3 cases — + genitive “on, upon”; + dative “upon”; + accusative “against”. 890 times in the GNT. EPIdermis is the skin on top. ἐπί is on, upon — and with the accusative, against: coming down upon somebody.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “from”; + dative “with”; + accusative “beside”.
extraQuiz.why: παρά — παρά takes 3 cases — + genitive “from”; + dative “with”; + accusative “beside”. 194 times in the GNT. PARAllel lines run beside each other; a PARAlegal works beside. With genitive from (beside someone), dative with, accusative beside.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “for”; + dative “at”; + accusative “to”.
extraQuiz.why: πρός — πρός takes 3 cases — + genitive “for”; + dative “at”; + accusative “to”. 700 times in the GNT. PROSelyte, one who has come to. With the accusative, to or toward — ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν — which is nearly all its uses.

extraQuiz.prompt: By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all
extraQuiz.greek: ἐν ᾧ θελήματι ἡγιασμένοι ἐσμὲν *διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς* τοῦ σώματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐφάπαξ (Heb 10:10)
extraQuiz.english: we have been sanctified *through the offering* of the body of Jesus Christ once for all
extraQuiz.why: διά is a preposition taking the genitive, so “through”. The phrase διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς hangs on the verb ἡγιασμένοι ἐσμέν: it says how we were sanctified — adverbial. (Asked about the word alone: διά + genitive, means or agency.)

extraQuiz.prompt: sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all
extraQuiz.greek: ἐν ᾧ θελήματι ἡγιασμένοι ἐσμὲν διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς τοῦ σώματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ *ἐφάπαξ* (Heb 10:10)
extraQuiz.english: sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ *once for all*
extraQuiz.why: ἐφάπαξ is an adverb (ἐπί + ἅπαξ, “once”), and it answers “when?” or “how often?” — once, for all time. That is time. It could be argued as manner (“in a once-for-all way”); time is the more natural reading, but worth checking in class.

extraQuiz.prompt: Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly
extraQuiz.greek: σπεῦσον καὶ ἔξελθε ἐν τάχει *ἐξ Ἰερουσαλήμ*, διότι οὐ παραδέξονταί σου μαρτυρίαν περὶ ἐμοῦ (Acts 22:18)
extraQuiz.english: Hurry and get *out of Jerusalem* quickly
extraQuiz.why: ἐξ is ἐκ before a vowel — a preposition taking the genitive, “out of”. ἐξ Ἰερουσαλήμ hangs on the imperative ἔξελθε and says where from: adverbial.

extraQuiz.prompt: because they will not accept your testimony about me
extraQuiz.greek: σπεῦσον καὶ ἔξελθε ἐν τάχει ἐξ Ἰερουσαλήμ, *διότι* οὐ παραδέξονταί σου μαρτυρίαν περὶ ἐμοῦ (Acts 22:18)
extraQuiz.english: *because* they will not accept your testimony about me
extraQuiz.why: διότι is a subordinating conjunction on the chart’s causal row: it gives the reason Paul must leave.

extraQuiz.prompt: they will not accept your testimony about me
extraQuiz.greek: διότι οὐ παραδέξονταί *σου* μαρτυρίαν περὶ ἐμοῦ (Acts 22:18)
extraQuiz.english: they will not accept *your* testimony about me
extraQuiz.why: σου is the genitive singular of σύ — a personal pronoun, “your”, here possessive on μαρτυρίαν.

extraQuiz.prompt: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.greek: *ἡμεῖς* δὲ ὀφείλομεν εὐχαριστεῖν τῷ θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ ὑμῶν (2 Thess 2:13)
extraQuiz.english: But *we* ought always to give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.why: ἡμεῖς is the personal pronoun “we”. ὀφείλομεν already says “we”, so the pronoun is emphatic: we, in contrast to those in 2:10–12.

extraQuiz.prompt: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.greek: ἡμεῖς *δὲ* ὀφείλομεν εὐχαριστεῖν τῷ θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ ὑμῶν (2 Thess 2:13)
extraQuiz.english: *But* we ought always to give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.why: δέ is a coordinating conjunction, and it is on the chart twice. Here it sets “we” against those who perish and believe the lie in 2:10–12, so adversative, “but”. A reader who takes it as a simple transition would call it copulative — worth hearing in class.

extraQuiz.prompt: give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.greek: ἡμεῖς δὲ ὀφείλομεν εὐχαριστεῖν τῷ θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ *ὑμῶν* (2 Thess 2:13)
extraQuiz.english: give thanks to God for *you*
extraQuiz.why: ὑμῶν is the genitive plural of σύ — personal pronoun, “you (all)”, the object of περί (“concerning, for”). ὑ has the u of YOU.
